_comment: The game's palette, taken from tiles2 rather than from the generator. tiles2 re-tints its whole tileset to the HUD's muted-forest theme via postprocess.palette (grass and dirt are colours the DESIGNER supplied); an earlier tiles 3.0 palette was measured from what PixelLab happens to produce, which is the generator's average and not an art direction at all. That is why 3.0 grass came out a bright yellow-green (#64b84d, hue 107deg) against 2.0's deep pine (hue 166deg) — 90 luminance apart. Values here are tiles2's ACTUAL APPEARANCE, not its configured target: 2.0 harmonises hue/sat while keeping each pixel's own value, so its art lands well above its target, and a flat 3.0 top has to match what the eye sees.

_wall_comment: The colour a material has as a WALL, which is NOT its top colour. The maintainer spotted that grass under an ice tile did not match grass under a grass tile: the same material was coming out four different greens depending on which cell drew it (hue 72-119, value 71-113). A wall needs one target per material, and it cannot simply be the top colour — a vertical face is lit differently, and the ratio is not even constant across materials (measured: grass 1.38x its top value, ice 0.70x). So hue and saturation come from the palette, and the VALUE is the median of what the generator actually draws for that material as a wall.

pair_tweaks._comment: Per-cell overrides for pairs the global classifier cannot decide. The maintainer, on black_rock over ice: 'It's almost as if it's time to do special tweaks for each different tile vs tile. That's a safe way to tweak when the postprocessing is already very good.' Used only where colour genuinely cannot separate the materials — black rock draws as dark navy (#03101c) and shaded ice as dark blue (#17212f).

black_rock__over__ice.note: the rock overhang on this pair hugs the top edge; claims deeper than a third of the face were shaded ice painted black — 'black rock on the left wall that should have been ice (not the overhang, but under the overhang)'

black_rock__over__grey_stone.note: claims stop at the lip (claim_depth) EXCEPT for drawn drips: below the lip a pixel is claimed iff it is strongly the top colour and connected to the lip through such pixels (deep_claim). The maintainer, on the beheaded overhangs: 'the overhang always starts from the edge ... Isn't it clear that this is still black_rock?' It is: measured on tile 17, drip pixels sit at 0.29-0.65 of the wall distance in the whitened space, the stones the cap protects at 1.49 — 0.7 splits them with margin on both sides. The wall below still takes the grey_stone ramp.

black_rock__over__dark_mud.note: the overhang, by the maintainer's definition: the top's own paint (cool — blue >= red; the mud is warm) connected to the top edge, allowed to jump the 1px drawn edge highlight; the highlight band itself is claimed with it and capped darker. Claims OVERWRITE the live wall paint, which is computed from the base classification — proven on all 31 candidates: zero pixels outside the claims differ from live ('WHAT WE HAVE IN GAME NOW HAS COLORED THE BOTTOM BROWN PERFECTLY ALREADY'). Approved: 'Your last post did it. It's Perfect now'

snow__over__brown_paving_stone.note: the snow drape's drawn underside kept its dark relief through substitution and read as leftover grey paving on the new brown wall (the maintainer circled it). Claimed pixels are floored to near the snow paint's own brightness: the shadow shape survives, but it is snow-bright.
